cur:catacombs-arles-eucharist.summary: Seven arched niches separated by columns each hold a standing, bearded figure; Christ stands at the centre among the apostles, several of whom carry offerings. The museum's name, 'the Eucharist', reflects the offering of gifts that runs through the procession.
facts: The museum calls it the 'Eucharistic sarcophagus' and dates it to the end of the 4th century.
cur:catacombs-arles-eucharist.notes: The identification of the central figure as Christ and of the Eucharistic theme follows the museum's naming; the figures are worn.

cur:catacombs2-saint-maximin-mary-magdal.summary: Very worn and mutilated, this columnar sarcophagus belongs to the type of the 'passion sarcophagi'. To the right of the central niche, which probably held a jewelled cross, Christ stands between two guards, raising his hand as he speaks, and in the next niche Pilate sits in judgement, his hand at his chin in doubt. At the left end Paul is led to martyrdom by an executioner drawing his sword; the next scene, an arrest between two soldiers, may show Peter or Paul.
facts: This is the sarcophagus venerated since the late 13th century as the tomb of Mary Magdalene, after Charles II of Anjou had the crypt searched in 1279.
According to French Wikipedia, its short sides show Judas's betrayal and Christ preaching, but they are hard to see in the present display.
The tomb now stands at the back of the crypt and serves as an altar.
cur:catacombs2-saint-maximin-mary-magdal.notes: Because of the heavy damage, the scenes are identified from the published description rather than from clear details in the photograph.

cur:manuscripts-stuttgart-psalter-psalm-.summary: On a rocky summit, Christ stands crowned and holding a cross-staff, while the hand of God reaches toward him from a fiery segment of heaven; below, two figures kneel or reach toward him from the slope. The image illustrates the verse written above it: 'The Lord hath said unto me, Thou art my Son; this day have I begotten thee'.
facts: The manuscript came to Württemberg under Duke Charles Eugene (its sale is first mentioned in 1787) and has been in the library at Stuttgart since at least 1818.
The Stuttgart Psalter was made around 820–830 at the abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés near Paris; its 168 leaves contain the psalms with 316 coloured miniatures set between the verses they illustrate.
cur:manuscripts-stuttgart-psalter-psalm-.notes: Image from the WLB digital facsimile (Public Domain Mark), showing the whole page with the miniature. The crowned figure lacks a clearly visible cross-nimbus at this resolution; identification follows the psalm verse and the Christological programme of the manuscript.

cur:manuscripts-stuttgart-psalter-psalm-.summary: On a green ground, Christ hangs on the cross wearing a loincloth, his head bowed, while a man kneels at the foot of the cross looking up and another stands pointing toward him. Above are the words of the psalm Christ prayed on the cross: 'O my God, I cry in the day time, but thou hearest not'.
facts: Its pictures interpret the psalms literally, historically or — very often — Christologically, as prophecies of the life of Christ.
The manuscript came to Württemberg under Duke Charles Eugene (its sale is first mentioned in 1787) and has been in the library at Stuttgart since at least 1818.
cur:manuscripts-stuttgart-psalter-psalm-.notes: Image from the WLB digital facsimile (Public Domain Mark), showing the whole page with the miniature.

cur:manuscripts2-otto-iii-blessing-child.summary: Under a hanging lamp in an arched frame, Christ stands larger than all around him and lays his hands on the heads of small children crowding at his feet, while apostles stand on either side. 'Suffer the little children to come unto me' is rendered with tender solemnity.
facts: The Gospels of Otto III has 276 leaves, twelve canon tables, a double-page portrait of the emperor, four evangelist portraits and 29 full-page miniatures of New Testament scenes; it was produced at Reichenau around 1000.
Its original cover still holds a 10th-century Byzantine ivory of the Dormition of the Virgin.
cur:manuscripts2-otto-iii-blessing-child.notes: Folio derived from the BSB image sequence (image 236); verify against the foliation on the page.

cur:monumental-santa-maria-in-domnica-ar.summary: At the summit of the arch above the apse, Christ is enthroned within a mandorla between two angels, while the twelve apostles stride towards him from both sides across a green ground; Moses and Elijah stand in the spandrels below. Seen together with the Virgin and Child in the apse beneath, the arch presents Christ in glory as the goal of the apostles' mission.
facts: Wikipedia describes the arch as showing Christ with two angels and the twelve apostles, with Moses and Elijah below, as part of Paschal I's 9th-century decoration.

links.label: Wikimedia Commons: Santa Maria in Domnica - Mosaics

cur:monumental-santa-maria-in-domnica-ar.notes: The photograph shows the whole apse; this entry concerns the arch above it, where Christ is relatively small in the image.

cur:monumental-san-clemente-madonna-nich.summary: In a shallow niche, the Virgin is shown frontally wearing a jewelled crown and earrings like a Byzantine empress, holding the Christ Child before her. The image is faded and damaged, but the imperial costume, also seen in the Maria Regina of Santa Maria Antiqua, presents the Mother of God as Queen of Heaven.
facts: Apart from Santa Maria Antiqua, the lower basilica of San Clemente holds the largest collection of early medieval wall paintings in Rome; the church was buried beneath the new basilica built around 1099–1120.
The figure's imperial regalia have even led some to suggest it was originally a portrait of an empress, such as Theodora, later adapted as the Virgin.
cur:monumental-san-clemente-madonna-nich.notes: Dating ranges from the 6th to the 9th century; the Commons photographer gives the 8th century.

walters:W.42.63R.summary: Inside a pink initial D on a gold ground, a fool carrying a staff or club confronts Christ, who stands at the right in a blue mantle with a halo, raising his hand. The initial opens Psalm 52 in the Latin numbering, 'Dixit insipiens in corde suo: non est Deus' ('The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God'), so the painter shows the fool face to face with the God he denies. Delicate pen flourishes in red and blue run down the margin.
facts: The psalter was made for Jernoul de Camphaing, whose name appears in a red inscription in the book (fol. 226r); the Walters places it in northeastern France, c. 1250–1275.

In illuminated psalters, historiated initials marked the beginnings of the major divisions of the Psalms and helped readers find their place in books without page numbers; Psalm 52 began one such division.
The manuscript was owned by the Paris binder and collector Léon Gruel before Henry Walters acquired it.
walters:W.42.63R.notes: Museum date 1250–1275; the 8th-century date in our data was an import error. Psalm 52 as a division opening is standard in the eightfold liturgical division of the Psalter.

Q19911431.summary: A small boat is tossed on a churning green sea while the terrified disciples bail, row and cry out. In the stern, wrapped in a halo of light, Christ sleeps peacefully, the one calm point in the storm. Delacroix, the great colourist of French Romanticism, turned the Gospel story into a meditation on faith amid chaos.
facts: Delacroix painted at least six versions of the subject, most of them in the 1850s, some showing a rowing boat and others a sailing boat; others are in the Walters Art Museum, the Portland Art Museum (Oregon), the Nelson-Atkins Museum and the Bührle Collection.
Vincent van Gogh saw this painting on display in Paris in 1886 and later wrote that it spoke a symbolic language through colour itself.
The Met's version came to the museum in 1929 with the celebrated bequest of Louisine Havemeyer.
